body.value: Summary of the introduction to chapter 2 in the *Bhagavadgītābhāṣya*: the chapter sets out Sāṅkhya — knowledge of the imperishable self — and only then turns to action. On this reading the teaching of action is preparatory: action performed without claim on its results purifies the mind, and it is knowledge (*jñāna*) that liberates. The order of the chapter is itself the argument.

Summary of Śaṅkara on 2.47: *adhikāra* — entitlement — extends to action and not to its fruit. The verse is addressed to one not yet qualified for the path of knowledge; renouncing the claim on results is what makes the mind fit for that path. The verse licenses action, but as preparation, not as the end.

Summary of Tilak, *Gītā Rahasya* (1915): the renunciation commanded here is of the *claim on the fruit*, not of the action. Read as a whole the Gītā is a summons to act in the world — Arjuna is told to fight, not to withdraw — and the reading that makes it a manual of renunciation reverses its plain sense. The Gītā's final teaching is *karmayoga*: energetic action, performed without attachment to result.

Summary of Gandhi, *Anāsakti Yoga* (1929): non-attachment to results is not a licence for any action whatever. One who has truly surrendered the fruit cannot act in anger or from self-interest, and so the verse carries *ahiṃsā* inside it. The activist reading is accepted as far as it goes — the Gītā does command action — but a reading that makes detachment compatible with violence has kept the letter and lost the discipline.

*karmaṇi eva adhikāraḥ te* — sandhi-joined in the written form. **adhikāra**: entitlement, jurisdiction, qualification to undertake something. A technical term of Mīmāṃsā ritual law, where it names who is eligible to perform a rite. The word denies a *claim*, not an outcome — which is the hinge every commentator in this stack turns on.

inputs.prompt: Read this verse against the three commentaries supplied. Report only what is visible in the Sanskrit or in the supplied layers. Do not attribute any claim to a commentator not supplied.

body.value:
**Machine-authored. Not a commentary.**

Observation from the three layers supplied: all three commentators accept that *adhikāra* denies a claim rather than an outcome, and all three then disagree about what a person is therefore free to do. Śaṅkara treats the freedom as freedom *from* the world, Tilak as freedom *for* action in it, Gandhi as freedom constrained by the character the discipline produces.

The verse itself supplies no scope marker — nothing in the Sanskrit says whether the release from claim applies to a monastic or a soldier. The commentators are not reading different words; they are supplying different premises about who the verse addresses. That gap in the text is where the whole 1,200-year argument sits.

*Produced from the four layers named in this record. No claim here is attributed to any commentator not listed.*

body.value: If Gandhi is right that the discipline changes what you are able to do, then the verse is not a rule at all — it is a description of a person. Does any of the three read it that way? Come back to this.

習，鳥數飛也。學之不已，如鳥數飛也。

(*xí*: a bird beating its wings again and again. To learn without ceasing is like a bird flying repeatedly.)

One character, glossed once — and for six centuries every examination candidate in China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam learned that 習 means *practice repeated until it becomes flight*, not *review*.

citation: 朱熹, 論語集注, 學而第一

body.value:
Summary of Ibn Kathīr on the *ḥurūf muqaṭṭaʿāt*, the disconnected letters opening this sūra: he records a spread of positions rather than settling one. Among them — that these letters belong to the *mutashābihāt*, whose meaning is known to God alone; that they are names or attributes of God; that they open the sūra to arrest the listener; and that they demonstrate the challenge of the Qur'ān, since it is composed of the same letters the Arabs themselves use.

The commentary here is *about three letters*. No system that can only annotate whole verses can represent it.

citation: Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-ʿAẓīm, opening of Sūrat al-Baqara

body.value: Letter-granularity test: a note anchored to the middle letter alone. Which of the positions Ibn Kathīr reports would even permit a question about one letter in isolation?

Summary of *Bereshit Rabbah* 1:10: why does the Torah open with *bet* rather than *alef*, the first letter? Because the shape of *bet* is closed on three sides and open only forward — teaching that one does not ask what is above, what is below, what came before; only what is from this point onward.

The reading is of the **shape of one letter**. Note that the span covers three codepoints — the consonant and its two combining marks — because splitting them would break the rendering and, in this tradition, the text.

Scribal apparatus, not exegesis: this *bet* is one of the *litterae majusculae* — written oversized in the scribal tradition. A plain Unicode edition cannot carry that information at all, which is why scribal features are a `variant` layer over the text rather than an attempt to encode them in it.

可道之道，可名之名，指事造形，非其常也。故不可道，不可名也。

(A way that can be spoken, a name that can be named — these point at affairs and shape forms, and so are not the constant. Therefore it cannot be spoken and cannot be named.)

A metaphysical reading: the opening denies that language reaches the Dao at all.

citation: 王弼, 老子道德經注, 第一章

body.value:
Summary of the Heshang Gong reading: the "way that can be spoken" is the way of classical learning and government instruction — a real way, but a taught one. The constant Dao is the way of spontaneity and long life, which is practised in the body rather than transmitted in words.

Same seven characters as Wang Bi, and a completely different book: not a metaphysics of language, but a manual of self-cultivation. This is the disagreement the layer switcher exists to show.

citation: 河上公章句, 體道第一

body.value:
The Mawangdui manuscripts read **恆** (*héng*, constant) where the received text reads **常** (*cháng*). The substitution is a naming taboo: 恆 was the personal name of Emperor Wen of Han (Liu Heng, r. 180–157 BCE), and scribes replaced it.

One character in the most-translated Chinese text in the world, changed by an emperor's name — and every English translation since inherits the substitution without mentioning it. This is exactly what a `variant` layer is for, and it is a single-character annotation.

citation: 馬王堆帛書老子 甲本・乙本

body.value: Summary of Śaṅkara on Īśā 1: *tena tyaktena bhuñjīthāḥ* — one protects the self through renunciation. The verse addresses the renunciate; the ritual life described from verse 2 onward is a separate path for those not qualified for knowledge. The two are not combined.

Summary of Aurobindo on Īśā 1: the verse says *enjoy* — the renunciation is of desire and of ownership, not of the world. Read as a command to withdraw, the sentence contradicts its own main verb.

Note the resonance with Gītā 2.47 (`gita:2.47`): the same argument, between the same two positions, on a different text. Cross-work stance tracking is what makes that visible.

Summary of Śaṅkara on the *pavamāna* mantras: the singer asks to be led from the unreal to the real, from darkness to light, from death to immortality — not to a different place, but to what he already is, uncovered.

One of the most recited passages in the corpus, and among the least contested. High popularity, low contestation: the two measures are independent, and the reading surface must not confuse them.

Summary of Matthew Henry on John 3:16: the exposition dwells on the scope of "the world" and on "whosoever" — the offer is not restricted in the text, and Henry reads that lack of restriction as the point of the verse.

The most-read verse in the corpus. It is in the sample specifically to show that the popularity axis and the contestation axis rank differently.

Summary of the Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā on verse 1: *mano-pubbaṅgamā* — mind goes before. The commentary supplies the occasion (the story of Cakkhupāla) rather than a definition, which is how this commentary works throughout: the verse is explained by the event that produced it.

The doctrinal point carried by the gloss is that what makes an act good or bad is the intention that precedes it, and the consequence follows the intention as the cart-wheel follows the ox. **Note what this is not saying:** the act is not evaluated by whether it succeeds.

Summary of Buddhaghosa on 279: *sabbe dhammā anattā* — all things whatsoever are without self. The commentary is careful about the scope of *sabbe dhammā*: unlike the two preceding verses, which say all *saṅkhāras* (conditioned things) are impermanent and unsatisfactory, this one says all *dhammās*, which includes the unconditioned. Nothing at all is a self.

This is the sharpest metaphysical divergence anywhere in the corpus. Set beside Śaṅkara on `upanishad:ISH.1`, the two are not answering differently — they are denying each other's subject.

Summary of Zhu Xi on 4.16: 義 (*yì*, rightness) is what heavenly principle requires; 利 (*lì*, gain) is what human desire pursues. The distinction between the noble person and the small person is not ability but which of the two the mind runs to first.

A position on the same question the Gītā and the Dhammapada address — whether an act is measured by what it yields — reached from a completely different starting point, and with a socially relational rather than soteriological frame.

citation: 朱熹, 論語集注, 里仁第四

body.value:
Summary of Matthew Henry on John 1:1: the *Logos* is named as the one by whom God is made known and by whom God speaks — speech is not a veil over the divine but the mode in which the divine is given.

Worth reading directly against `daodejing:1`, whose opening sentence says that a way that can be spoken is not the constant way. Two texts, both at the opening of their book, taking opposite positions on whether the ultimate can be uttered. Neither is refuting the other — they never met — and the resonance map records this as a **divergence with a shared question**, not as a dispute.
